text: How much electrical push the battery has. A healthy battery reads about 12.6V with the engine off, and 13.8 to 14.7V running. You check it with a cheap multimeter (about $15) or free at a parts store.
Pounds per square inch: a measure of pressure, the same unit as tire pressure. A shop uses a gauge to measure it.
Millimeters. 3 mm is about the thickness of two stacked coins.
Milliamps: a tiny amount of electricity. Used to check if something drains the battery while parked.
Foot-pounds: how tight a bolt should be. Set with a torque wrench, which clicks when it's right.
Engine temperature in Fahrenheit. Normal is the middle of your temperature gauge.
Grams per second: how much air goes into the engine. Only shown on a scan tool.
Inches. 1/8 inch is about the thickness of a coin; 1/32 inch is about a paper clip wire.
A cheap handheld tool (about $15) that measures volts. Touch the red probe to + and black to - on the battery.
The shiny metal disc behind each wheel. The brake pads squeeze it to stop the vehicle.
The parts that press on the rotors to stop the wheels. They wear down like an eraser and get replaced.
The clamp at each wheel that squeezes the brake pads onto the rotor.
The brake fluid tank under the hood, usually on the driver's side near the windshield. It has MIN and MAX lines.
Thin metal tubes that carry brake fluid to each wheel. Rust can eat through them.
Anti-lock brakes: keeps wheels from locking up in hard stops. Its light on the dash means that system has a problem.
Parts inside each wheel that let it spin smoothly. Worn ones hum or growl.
The long rubber belt on the front of the engine that turns the alternator, power steering pump and water pump.
A spring-loaded pulley that keeps the belt tight.
A wheel the belt rides on.
Recharges the battery and powers the electrics while the engine runs.
The small motor that spins the engine when you turn the key. The solenoid is the switch on it that clicks.
Something that keeps using power with everything off and drains the battery overnight.
Makes the spark that lights the fuel in each cylinder. Wears out and gets replaced.
Turns battery power into the big spark for the spark plug. One per cylinder on most trucks.
Where the fuel burns to make power. A V8 has 8 of them, numbered.
When a cylinder doesn't fire properly. The engine shakes and runs rough.
A shop test that checks each cylinder seals well. Big differences mean internal engine wear.
A sensor in the air intake tube that measures air going into the engine.
Air getting into the engine through a crack instead of through the air filter.
How much the engine computer is adding or removing fuel to correct the mix. Shown on a scan tool.
Pushes gas from the tank to the engine. You can often hear it hum for 2 seconds when you turn the key on.
Catches dirt in the gas. On older GM trucks it's on the frame under the driver's side.
A test port like a tire valve on the fuel rail. A shop hooks a pressure gauge to it.
A valve that keeps the engine at the right temperature by controlling coolant flow.
The colored liquid (often green or orange) that carries heat away from the engine. Check it only when the engine is cold.
The big finned part at the very front that cools the coolant.
A seal inside the engine. When it fails, coolant and oil can mix. An expensive repair.
Makes the engine fan spin harder when the engine is hot. On trucks it's behind the radiator.
Liquids your vehicle uses: brake, transmission, power steering, coolant, oil. Each has its own dipstick or tank.
Connects the engine to an automatic transmission, like a clutch.
The shaft that drives a front wheel. The rubber boot keeps grease in; once it tears, the joint wears out.
Flexible joints at the ends of the driveshaft (the long tube under the truck).
The long spinning tube under the truck that sends power to the wheels.
A tiny nipple where you pump in grease with a grease gun.
Small weights on the rim that make the wheel spin evenly so it doesn't shake.
The angles of your wheels. A shop adjusts them so the vehicle drives straight and tires wear evenly.
Steering arms that connect the steering to the front wheels.
Pivot joints that let the front wheels turn and move up and down.
Steering linkage parts on GM trucks that wear out and cause loose steering.
They stop the vehicle from bouncing after bumps.
The front spring on many 4WD GM trucks: a steel bar that twists.
The pipe that bolts to the side of the engine and collects exhaust. Its bolts can break and cause a tick.
Measures oxygen in the exhaust so the engine can fine-tune the fuel mix.
Cleans the exhaust. Expensive; a misfire left too long can ruin it.
A valve that sends a little exhaust back into the engine to cut pollution. Can clog with carbon.
The system that traps gas fumes from the tank. A loose gas cap is the most common cause of its codes.
Listens for engine knock. On GM V8s they sit under the intake manifold and corrode when water gets in.
The engine-shaped light on the dash. It means the computer saved a trouble code; a scanner reads it.
A small tool that plugs in under the dash and reads trouble codes. Most parts stores scan for free.
A letter plus 4 characters (like P0300) that the computer saves when it notices a problem.
Metal stands that hold the vehicle up safely. Never get under a vehicle held up only by a jack.
A long stick under the hood (usually yellow handle) that shows the oil level.
The gas inside the A/C that makes the air cold.
The front of the A/C pump. When the A/C is on, its center should spin.
A flap behind the dash that mixes hot and cold air.
A thick wire or braided strap connecting the engine and body back to the battery's negative side.
A shop test that finds bad connections by measuring lost voltage across a wire.
How much a rotor wobbles as it spins. Measured with a dial gauge.
Engine speed, shown on the tachometer gauge.
Four-wheel drive: the front wheels also get power when it's engaged.
Raising the truck with a kit. It changes angles on the steering and driveline, so those parts wear faster.
The part on top of the engine that feeds air to each cylinder.
A small valve and hoses that vent fumes from inside the engine. Cracked hoses cause vacuum leaks.
The big round can behind the brake fluid tank that makes the brake pedal easy to push.
Pumps coolant through the engine. A leak from its small 'weep hole' means it's failing.
A small radiator behind the dash that heats the cab.
Changes gears so the engine can drive the wheels at different speeds.
Lean = too much air for the fuel. Rich = too much fuel for the air.
The engine computer.
